card.name: Yayue
card.tagline: The formal, ritualized music and dance of the ancient Chinese imperial court.
card.profile: Yayue, or 'elegant music,' served as the formal, ritualized representation of aristocratic power in ancient China. Established in the Western Zhou dynasty, it functioned as a moral and political tool, distinguishing the refined courtly sphere from popular entertainment. Today, it exists as a reconstructed tradition, preserved in Confucian rituals in Taiwan and studied as a historical foundation for East Asian court arts.
card.insight: In 1116, Emperor Huizong gifted 428 instruments and 572 costumes to Korea, effectively creating a time capsule of ancient Chinese melodies that were later lost in their homeland.
card.profile_long:
Yayue, literally 'elegant music,' functioned as the primary ceremonial music and dance of the Chinese imperial court and temples for millennia. Established during the Western Zhou dynasty, it was conceived not merely as entertainment, but as a moral and political instrument. Confucius championed yayue as a tool for self-cultivation and stable governance, contrasting it sharply with the 'decadent' popular music of the state of Zheng. The tradition was deeply integrated with the rites and laws of the state, serving to reinforce the social hierarchy and the legitimacy of the emperor.

The performance of yayue was characterized by extreme rigidity and formal structure. Orchestras were divided into two distinct ensembles representing the yin and yang: the smaller 'dengge' ensemble performed on building terraces, while the larger 'gongxian' ensemble occupied the courtyard. In the courtyard, musicians were arranged in five directions, with wind instruments in the center, bronze bells and stone chimes on the four sides, and drums at the four corners. The number of dancers was strictly regulated by the rank of the patron, with the emperor entitled to 64 dancers arranged in eight rows of eight, while lower officials were restricted to smaller configurations.

Instruments were categorized by the eight materials used in their construction: silk, bamboo, wood, stone, metal, clay, gourd, and hide. Notable instruments included the guqin, stone chimes (bianqing), and bronze bells (bianzhong). The music itself was typically slow, stately, and monophonic, with little rhythmic variety. When accompanied by song, phrases were structured into four to eight beats. Dances were divided into two categories: civil dances, where performers held a flute and feather plume, and military dances, involving a shield and battleaxe.

Following the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, the tradition largely disappeared from public practice in China. However, the tradition survived in modified forms in neighboring countries, such as the aak in Korea, which preserved melodies from the Song dynasty. Modern efforts to reconstruct yayue began in Taiwan in the 1960s and in mainland China in the 1990s. These contemporary performances often utilize modern instruments, leading to ongoing debates regarding the authenticity of the revived forms compared to their ancient predecessors.

card.sacred_note: Yayue is intrinsically linked to Confucian rites, ancestor worship, and ceremonies honoring Heaven and Earth; it is considered a formal, moral, and political instrument of the state.

sections.origins_and_history: Established in the Western Zhou dynasty, yayue was commissioned by the Duke of Zhou. It incorporated shamanistic traditions and early folk music. It remained central to imperial ceremonies until the end of the Qing dynasty, with major developments occurring during the Song dynasty.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are strictly categorized as civil or military. Civil dancers hold a yue flute in the left hand and a feather plume in the right. Military dancers hold a shield in the left hand and a battleaxe in the right. The number of dancers is determined by the rank of the host, ranging from 64 for the emperor to 16 for lesser officers.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is monophonic, slow, and stately, with 4-8 beats per phrase. Instruments are classified into eight material categories: silk (guqin, se), bamboo (dizi, xiao, paixiao, chi), wood (zhu, yu), stone (bianqing), metal (bianzhong, fangxiang), clay (xun), gourd (sheng, yu), and hide (gu).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occurred on palace terraces or in courtyards. Musicians and dancers wore formal court attire. The spatial arrangement followed five directions, with the orchestra split into yin (terrace) and yang (courtyard) ensembles.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Yayue was performed for ceremonies honoring Heaven, Earth, ancestors, and gods. It was also used for diplomatic meetings, archery contests, hunting expeditions, and celebrations following military victories.
sections.notable_figures: Duke of Zhou (founder), Confucius (philosopher who championed yayue), Emperor Huizong of Song (patron who gifted instruments to Korea), Chen Yang (author of the Yueshu).
sections.regional_variants: Gagaku (Japan), Aak (Korea), Nhã nhạc (Vietnam). These forms share the same characters but have evolved independently from the Chinese original.
sections.lineage: Directly linked to the Six Great Dances of the Zhou dynasty; influenced the development of Confucian ritual music across East Asia.

claims.text: The basic conventions of yayue were established in the Western Zhou.
Confucius considered yayue to be the kind of music that is good and beneficial.
In 1116, a gift of 428 yayue instruments as well as 572 costumes and dance objects was given to Korea by Emperor Huizong.
The court yayue orchestra may be divided into two separate ensembles that may represent the yin and yang.
The emperor may have the largest number of musicians and dancers (64 dancers in eight rows of eight).
In civil dance, the dancers hold a yue flute (籥) in their left hands and a feather plume (羽) in their right.
Yayue was still performed as part of a Confucian ritual in China until the Communist takeover in 1949, where it disappeared as a practice.
